data.title: Weak Domain Password Policy
data.summary: The password policy permitted passwords short enough to be cracked quickly and did not screen against known-breached or predictable values, so a significant proportion of account passwords were recoverable from captured hashes.
data.description:
Password policy determines how much of a captured hash set becomes usable credentials. Length is the dominant factor; complexity rules mostly shape passwords into predictable patterns — a capital at the start, a digit and a symbol at the end — that cracking rules model directly.

Seasonal and company-name passwords are the common result, and they are exactly what spraying tries first. Mandatory periodic expiry worsens this, producing incremented variants that are trivially guessed from a previous password.

Modern guidance from NIST reverses the old advice: longer minimums, no composition rules, no scheduled expiry, and screening against breach corpora.
data.recommendation:
* Set a minimum length of at least 14 characters for users and considerably more for privileged and service accounts.
* Screen new passwords against a breached-password corpus and a custom list of company-specific terms.
* Remove scheduled expiry; change passwords on evidence of compromise.
* Deploy multi-factor authentication, which matters more than any policy parameter.
* Encourage passphrases and provide a password manager.
data.short_recommendation: Raise minimum length and screen against breached passwords.
